gist: Data belonging to more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security personnel was leaked online.
Hackers obtained employee records, operational names, and surveillance tools, reportedly via Okta.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A group calling itself the Department of Peace accessed and leaked details of over 41,000 Department of Homeland Security personnel. Distributed Denial of Secrets published the database, named Icepick. Outlets disagree on exact numbers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, citing nearly 6,600, about 6,600, 7,000, or roughly 10,000 records. While activists claim the data came via Okta, Okta denies its systems were compromised.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The breach exposes organisational charts, undercover operations, and surveillance tools used across agencies including border and immigration enforcement. It follows controversial immigration crackdowns, fatal shootings by agents, and official efforts to conceal staff identities while seeking to unmask public critics.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Homeland Security stated it is actively addressing the potential breach to protect personnel and will update the public when further information becomes available.

Applicants must meet strict conditions regarding income, language, and no criminal record.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government plans to double the standard length of time migrants must live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement from five to 10 years. A 10-year pathway requires earning at least £12,571 for five of the seven years before settlement. Shorter qualifying periods of three or five years apply to specific groups, including high earners, certain care workers, skilled public service workers, and people with British National (Overseas) status. Conversely, migrants who claimed certain benefits or breached rules face a 20-year wait. Additional conditions include having no criminal record, speaking good English, owing no taxpayer debt, and having a record of National Insurance contributions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, a 45 percent year-over-year increase. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The data centre business now accounts for approximately 63 percent of AMD's total quarterly revenue. Meanwhile, component shortages linked to AI demand are impacting consumer system pricing.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, India's costliest film, has been released worldwide. The two-part production adapts the Hindu epic, featuring Ranbir Kapoor as Ram and Yash as Ravana. It incorporates Hollywood visual effects and a score by AR Rahman and Hans Zimmer.

sections.text: The film is a significant cultural moment, retelling a story central to Hindu identity. Critics are divided; some praise its spectacular scale and adventure, while others criticise inconsistent acting, clunky action, and the use of AI for lip movements. It follows previous adaptations that have faced controversy.

sections.text: Major technology companies reported record capital expenditure plans for AI infrastructure, totalling hundreds of billions. PACs remain committed to future election spending despite recent losses for several backed candidates.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Political action committees supporting and opposing the AI industry spent millions of dollars during the midterm elections. Groups like American Mission and Building the Future backed various candidates, many of whom lost. Conversely, groups advocating for stronger AI safeguards, such as Public First and Guardrails Alliance, also experienced mixed outcomes in their efforts to influence race results.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The spending reflects a broader struggle over whether Congress should establish a national AI framework or allow states to maintain their own safeguards. Industry groups aim to shape policy agendas, while opposition groups seek to make accepting AI-related funding a political liability for candidates.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Both sides intend to continue their involvement in future elections. Leading the Future plans to maintain its spending strategy for 2028, while the Guardrails Alliance remains committed to opposing candidates supported by the AI industry.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: East Asia has experienced a series of severe typhoons exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern. Storms such as Champi, Dolphin, and Saudel have caused widespread disruption, including flight cancellations, power outages, and flooding across China, Japan, the Philippines, and Taiwan. These typhoons are forming further east and intensifying due to record-high sea surface temperatures.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The current El Niño is forecast to be the strongest in living memory, with Pacific temperatures reaching record levels. This climate phenomenon increases the intensity and rainfall of storms, threatening infrastructure, food security, and public safety. Climatologists warn that higher temperatures significantly amplify rainfall, posing severe risks to vulnerable regions.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The El Niño pattern is expected to persist until February or March. Countries are preparing for continued disruptions by upgrading warning systems, stockpiling essentials, and supporting farmers. Authorities remain concerned as sea surface temperatures are predicted to rise further.

gist: Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives may cause vital micronutrient deficiencies.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study published in the Lancet Planetary Health indicates that replacing dairy products with plant-based alternatives may lead to deficiencies in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12. Researchers modelled the impact of substituting dairy with non-dairy milks, yoghurts and cheeses, noting that many current products lack sufficient fortification.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Iodine is essential for thyroid function, metabolism and brain development. The study highlights that teenage girls and women of childbearing age are particularly at risk, as they already have low iodine intake. While some manufacturers fortify their products, there is no formal requirement to do so, leading to concerns about public health outcomes as plant-based diets grow in popularity.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers suggest that requiring all non-dairy alternatives to be fortified with iodine could prevent average declines in nutrient intake. Dietitians recommend that consumers check labels for fortification and consider other dietary sources of iodine.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A proposed study involving 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau was cancelled after facing accusations of being unethical and neocolonial. The trial, funded by the US, planned to withhold a hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants. Following public outcry and government intervention, the trial was prohibited, and police seized a batch of vaccines from the Bandim Health Project research centre.

sections.text: The trial sparked international criticism because it withheld a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization in a country where the infection is widespread. The controversy also highlighted tensions regarding research ethics and the influence of US vaccine policy.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Guinea-Bissau officials are considering introducing the birth-dose vaccine into the routine immunisation schedule earlier than the previously planned 2028 date. Meanwhile, police investigations into the seized vaccines and the circumstances surrounding the research centre continue.

sections.text: Italian chef Davide Tamburella was sacked from a Brisbane restaurant called La Costa in May after refusing to provide a ham and pineapple pizza for a function. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A three-judge panel ruled that the medical drama The Pitt shares sufficient similarities with the series ER to allow a lawsuit to proceed. Sherri Crichton, widow of ER creator Michael Crichton, claims the show violates a contractual provision prohibiting reboots without consent. While Warner Bros argued the similarities were generic to hospital dramas, the court found enough evidence to support a prima facie case. The court dismissed claims against individual producers Noah Wyle, John Wells, and R Scott Gemmill, citing insufficient evidence of their awareness regarding potential contractual violations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case centres on the protection of intellectual property and contractual rights for creators and their estates. It highlights the legal tension between developing original content and the potential for derivative works to infringe upon existing agreements.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Joshua Wong, a prominent pro-democracy activist, received a 10-year prison sentence in Hong Kong. He pleaded guilty to foreign collusion charges, specifically for conspiring to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions and blockades against China. The judge described his actions as grave and part of a scheme to seek foreign interference. Wong, who is already serving time for a separate subversion conviction, appeared in court wearing a dark blue shirt and glasses.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The sentencing highlights the ongoing application of Hong Kong's national security law. Critics, including Amnesty International, argue the law is used to suppress political dissent and silence opposition. Conversely, the Hong Kong chief executive and China's foreign ministry maintain the ruling protects national security and stability. The case has drawn international condemnation, with the US consulate calling for Wong's release, while Beijing has warned against foreign interference in its judicial affairs.

gist: Geologists have ruled out north-east Scotland as the origin of Stonehenge's Altar Stone.

Researchers continue to search for the stone's origin across other potential regions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A team of international geologists conducted a comprehensive investigation into the origin of the Altar Stone at Stonehenge. Previous research had suggested the stone originated from north-east Scotland, but new testing of samples has ruled this location out. The study, which involved analysing stone fragments and comparing them to geological outcrops, concluded that the source remains an enigma.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Identifying the origin of the Altar Stone would provide significant insights into the lives and capabilities of Neolithic people. Understanding where the stone was sourced helps experts reconstruct the journey of the six-tonne slab to Salisbury Plain and reveals the long-distance connections that existed thousands of years ago.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers are continuing their search for the stone's origin. Experts suggest the Altar Stone may have come from other parts of Scotland, northern England, or Ireland. The team maintains that ruling out potential source areas is a vital part of the ongoing geological detective process.

timeline.text: South West Water’s failure to fix leaks ‘putting customer supplies at risk’

gist: Regulators warn South West Water over persistent failure to address significant pipe leakage.
Leakage issues threaten customer water supplies amid ongoing severe drought conditions in the region.
The company must submit an action plan to address these leaks within six weeks.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Regulators and the government issued a joint letter to South West Water regarding seven years of failure to meet leakage reduction targets. The company currently loses over 113 million litres of water daily, a figure that has increased since last year. This occurs while large parts of England remain in drought, with reservoir levels at sites like Wimbleball reaching critically low points.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The failure to fix leaks places customer water supplies at risk, potentially leading to supply cuts, school closures and economic losses for thousands in Devon. Regulators state that these shortcomings are unacceptable while the company asks households to reduce usage. Furthermore, the situation threatens environmental damage through emergency river abstraction.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: South West Water is required to submit an action plan to the government and regulators within six weeks to address its leakage performance. Meanwhile, the government is establishing new regional water councils to help set priorities for water companies and shape future infrastructure investment.

fivew: Ofwat, the Environment Agency, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, and South West Water.

gist: Campaigners argue reparations should focus on repair rather than just simple cash payments.
Proposed reparatory justice includes climate resilience, public inquiries and returning cultural artefacts.
Advocates seek to address the ongoing legacy of slavery through systemic and structural changes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Campaigners are calling for a broader approach to reparatory justice regarding the legacy of slavery. They argue that focusing solely on cash payments is unhelpful and overlooks the core goal of repair. Proposals include building climate-resilient infrastructure, establishing a national commission of inquiry into Britain's colonial history, and returning cultural artefacts held in European collections.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Proponents suggest that current discussions often frame reparations within sustainable development goals, which allows for a discretionary approach rather than an obligation. Campaigners believe that a formal reparatory framework is necessary to address the root causes of broken systems and to restore relationships. They emphasise that understanding the history of the British empire is essential for communities to heal.

sections.text: Democrats gained hundreds of state legislative seats, winning control of chambers in states like Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. sections.text: State legislatures have become critical arenas for policy as federal gridlock persists. Democratic control allows the party to pursue legislative agendas on issues like abortion access, minimum wage, and climate change, reversing years of conservative policy-making in these states.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Incoming Democratic majorities are preparing to address legislative backlogs. gist: A former SAS officer denies the unit conducted shoot-to-kill missions during the Troubles.
The government defends its legacy legislation, while victims' groups criticise the process.
Disagreements persist regarding whether IRA members could have been arrested during specific operations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Former SAS officer George Simm denied that the unit operated under a shoot-to-kill policy during the Troubles. Simm, who led an ambush in 1988 that resulted in the deaths of three IRA members, stated that soldiers only fired when under direct attack. He criticised the government for failing to support veterans regarding legacy legislation. Conversely, relatives of those killed by the SAS argue that the soldiers could have arrested the men instead of killing them, describing the events as pre-planned shoot-to-kill operations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The debate highlights ongoing tensions surrounding the legacy of the conflict in Northern Ireland. While the government claims its Troubles Bill provides effective safeguards for veterans, groups like Relatives for Justice argue that the legislation prioritises the interests of those who killed over the rights of victims and survivors.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Amazon and Uber have partnered to integrate Uber Eats into the Amazon platform. Prime members in the US can now order restaurant meals directly via the Amazon app or website without needing a separate Uber account. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This collaboration marks Amazon's return to restaurant delivery after previously closing its own service. By partnering, Amazon avoids the high costs of building a delivery network from scratch. For Uber, the deal provides access to millions of Prime subscribers, helping the company compete against its larger rival, DoorDash.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: It remains uncertain if this benefit will significantly influence Prime subscriber behaviour. While the deal removes delivery fees for orders over twenty-five dollars, other costs such as service fees, tips, and menu markups remain, potentially limiting the appeal for casual or solo diners.

gist: Met Police shifts officers from major events to local communities due to financial pressures.
Sir Mark Rowley warns forces must be slashed or face inevitable decline and failure.
A government review proposes cutting the number of police forces from 43 to nine.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Metropolitan Police shifted officers away from major events to boost local policing, freeing up thousands of shifts. Meanwhile, a government-ordered review recommended cutting police forces in England and Wales from 43 to as few as nine regional super forces.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Police leaders warn that the current model is broken and public confidence is falling. However, police chiefs remain divided over whether massive regional forces are the right solution.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The review by Bernard Hogan-Howe is set to be published before Christmas, with a government white paper due in the new year.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Democrats secured control of the House and Senate following midterm elections. Voters across various states supported local measures to restrict data centre construction, with 43 out of 44 local moratoria passing. Candidates who campaigned on holding AI companies accountable saw success, while some Republican efforts to prevent state-level AI restrictions appear to have stalled.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The results signal a shift toward stricter oversight of the AI industry. Concerns regarding electricity costs, noise pollution, and local infrastructure have turned data centres into a bipartisan political issue. Industry experts suggest this environment will make future construction more difficult and likely lead to increased legislative efforts focused on tech accountability and AI safety.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: AI companies face the prospect of increased regulation and potential delays in infrastructure projects. Incoming leaders have indicated plans to call CEOs to testify. While some analysts suggest a slowdown could help prevent an AI market bubble, others anticipate a period of significant legislative hurdles for the technology sector.

sections.text: Nigel Farage held a press conference at Billingsgate fish market to introduce Angus MacIntyre as Reform's armed forces spokesperson. MacIntyre, a former wing commander with 40 years of service, was presented as an expert to address national defence concerns. During the event, Farage criticised current defence spending and global security, while MacIntyre described contemporary military attitudes as being influenced by Marxist ideology.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The appointment highlights Reform's attempt to establish a stronger position on defence, a subject the party has previously been criticised for neglecting. However, the selection of MacIntyre has faced scrutiny, with questions raised about his career progression within the RAF and his alignment with Farage's broader political views on international relations, including the war in Ukraine and relations with Nato.

gist: US tech shares plummeted as investors fear stricter AI regulation following midterm election results.
The Nasdaq index entered correction territory amid concerns over massive artificial intelligence spending.
Chip manufacturers experienced significant losses as market volatility reached its highest level in months.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US tech shares experienced a sharp decline, with the Nasdaq index falling by up to 5% on Thursday. This drop pushed the index into correction territory, marking its worst performance in 18 months. Chip stocks were particularly affected, with significant losses reported for companies like SanDisk and Western Digital. Market volatility, measured by the VIX, surged by 40%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Investors are concerned that Democratic successes in midterm elections will lead to tougher regulation of the artificial intelligence industry. There is specific anxiety regarding the expansion of datacentres, which faced opposition in local ballots and is expected to face scrutiny from Democratic governors. Analysts suggest the market is shifting focus from the potential of AI to the costs associated with its development.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Market participants are looking for signs of stability following the sell-off. Analysts warn that the pace of datacentre construction is likely to slow as the political landscape creates hurdles for tech legislation over the next two years.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: NHS England recorded over 373,000 cancer diagnoses in 2024, averaging 1,021 cases per day. While early-stage detection rates improved slightly, the health service continues to miss key performance targets for urgent referrals and treatment commencement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Rising demand, driven by an ageing population and factors like obesity, places significant pressure on NHS services. Experts warn that failing to meet waiting time targets and late-stage diagnoses negatively impact patient outcomes and survival chances.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Calls are mounting for the government to provide additional support, including specialist staff and equipment. Organisations emphasise the need for continued investment in early detection programmes and addressing persistent health inequalities to ensure equitable access to care.

timeline.text: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices

gist: A decade-old vulnerability dubbed *sshole affects some configurations of Alpine Linux and other distributions.
The flaw allows attackers to log into certain passwordless accounts with no password.
Exploitation requires specific conditions involving OpenSSH, musl, PAM, and password hashing configurations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A vulnerability in the interaction between OpenSSH, musl, and specific configurations allows attackers to log into Linux devices without a password. Alpine maintainers and security firm Checkpoint reported that the flaw works every time with a single connection when specific conditions are met, including passwordless account settings and particular password hashing functions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The consequences of the vulnerability are high because attackers reaching the SSH port can gain access without knowing any password. However, root accounts are safe under default settings, though accounts with sudo or doas rights can still elevate privileges.

gist: Aircraft engine turbine blades are grown as a single crystal through a specialized casting process.
Only a handful of companies worldwide can produce these single crystal turbine blades.
China is striving to master the technology, while Western manufacturers maintain a major advantage.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Aircraft engines use hundreds of turbine blades grown from a molten metal alloy into a single crystal. Only a few companies and five countries have perfected this complex manufacturing process. GE Aerospace announced it would acquire its turbine blade supplier, and Rolls-Royce said it would invest in its blade casting facility.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: These hardy blades withstand extreme temperatures and mechanical stresses. The single crystal structure is essential for blade performance, allowing engines to run efficiently. Demand is huge and supply chains are volatile, making the technology a critical component for aircraft manufacturing.

sections.heading: What happens next

gist: Universities in England used below-average salaries for student loan repayment examples on websites.
Some information provided to prospective students was described as misleading.
The Department for Education and several universities pledged to review their information.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The BBC found that 12 universities in England only used below-average salaries in student loan repayment examples on their websites. Some sites also featured inaccurate details about repayment thresholds and write-off dates, while the Department for Education's website lacked real-world examples for Plan 5 students.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier said the information was misleading and compared repayments to minor expenses. Graduates may face higher monthly repayments as their salaries increase over time, meaning initial low estimates can give a false impression of future costs.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Department for Education stated it would review the information it provides and work with universities. Several universities have already updated their websites or are reviewing their content following the BBC's findings.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Liverpool lost 3-2 to Fenerbahce in Istanbul after conceding three goals from set-pieces. Despite taking the lead twice through Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak, Liverpool failed to maintain their advantage. Fenerbahce, managed by interim boss Dirk Kuyt, secured the win with goals from Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown, and Vedat Muriqi.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The defeat represents a significant setback for Liverpool, who have now lost twice in four days. It is the latest point in a major European game that Liverpool have led before losing. For Fenerbahce, the result is a historic victory against an English side, providing a morale boost during a difficult season.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A semi-final under-20s match between Uberlandia and Mamore in Brazil was abandoned after 51 red cards were issued. A brawl began in the second half when a player taunted the opposing bench, leading to confrontations involving players and staff. The referee halted the game for 40 minutes before abandoning it due to the scale of the disorder and damage caused to the stadium.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The incident set a new world record for red cards in a single match, surpassing the previous record of 36. Significant damage was reported at the Parque do Sabia Stadium, including broken doors, windows, and furniture, requiring the intervention of military police.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Uberlandia has conceded the second leg of the semi-final, citing a gesture of fair play because Mamore lacks sufficient available players. Mamore will advance to the final, while Uberlandia will compete in the third-place match.

articles.title: Ocon dropped - is it the end of his F1 career?
articles.standfirst: Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after falling out with Haas. Andrew Benson looks at what the future holds for the Frenchman.

timeline.text: Ocon dropped - is it the end of his F1 career?

gist: Esteban Ocon was dropped by Haas for the rest of the season after a falling-out.
The decision follows a history of team friction and being outperformed by team-mates.
Ocon now faces a period on the sidelines with little prospect of returning.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Esteban Ocon was dropped by Haas following a disagreement with team principal Ayao Komatsu after practice in Mexico City. Ocon had objected over the radio to a tyre strategy change. While L'Equipe reported the meeting ended physically, Ocon categorically rejected any physical violence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Ten years into his Formula 1 career, Ocon has a reputation for friction with teams and team-mates. Having been outperformed by team-mates like Oliver Bearman, and with new talent emerging, this departure may signal the end of his Formula 1 career.

fivew: Esteban Ocon was dropped by Haas for the remainder of the F1 season.
A falling-out with team principal Ayao Komatsu following a disagreement over tyre strategy.
